lead: A continuous beam runs over three or more supports. The bending moments at its supports are unknown, so equilibrium alone cannot find them. Clapeyron's three-moment equation links the moments at three consecutive supports in one line. Write it for each pair of spans and you get simultaneous equations for the whole beam. Aircraft floor beams, engine mounts and wing spar splices often use such continuous runs. Moment distribution reaches the same support moments by iteration.
prereq: You need statically indeterminate beams for releasing a redundant, and free bending moment diagrams of simply supported beams.

blocks.text: Take three consecutive supports A, B, C. Span AB = L₁ and span BC = L₂, in metres. M<sub>A</sub>, M<sub>B</sub>, M<sub>C</sub> are the support moments, in kN·m. Use sagging positive and hogging negative. The free bending moment diagram is what the span would carry if it were a simple beam.
M<sub>A</sub> L₁ + 2M<sub>B</sub>(L₁ + L₂) + M<sub>C</sub> L₂ = −6(A₁x̄₁/L₁ + A₂x̄₂/L₂)
blocks.where: A₁, A₂ are the areas of the free bending moment diagrams of the two spans, in kN·m²; x̄₁, x̄₂ are the distances of their centroids from the outer supports A and C, in metres.

blocks.text: The right side is negative for downward loads. A simply supported end has M = 0; a fixed end has M unknown and needs one more equation.

The equation assumes the same EI along both spans, supports at one level with no settlement, and loads in the plane of the beam. A change of EI between spans or a sinking support adds terms to both sides.
Two load cases cover most questions. For a uniform load w₁ on L₁ and w₂ on L₂, the right side becomes

blocks.where: w₁, w₂ are the uniform loads in kN/m on the two spans.

blocks.text: For a central point load P₁ on L₁ and P₂ on L₂, it becomes

blocks.where: P₁, P₂ are the point loads in kN at midspan of the two spans.

items: Write the equation for each set of three consecutive supports.
Put M = 0 at every simple end.
Keep M unknown at every fixed or continuous support.
Substitute the free-diagram area and centroid distance.
Solve the simultaneous equations for the unknown support moments.

blocks.text: Measure x̄₁ from A and x̄₂ from C, not from B. A fixed end adds an unknown M. Treat the fixed end as a continuous support with an imaginary span of zero length and no load beyond it; writing the equation across that span gives the extra equation.

figure.caption: Worked example 1: two spans, 6 m and 4 m, under 10 kN/m. The three-moment equation gives M<sub>B</sub> = −35 kN·m. The final diagram (solid) is each span’s free parabola (dashed, peaks 45 and 20 kN·m) less the straight line through the support moments, leaving sagging peaks of 29.2 and 6.3 kN·m.

spec.aria: A two-span beam on supports A, B and C at 0, 6 and 10 metres under a uniform load. Below, dashed free bending moment parabolas peaking at 45 and 20, a dotted closing line down to minus 35 at B, and the solid final moment diagram with sagging peaks of 29.2 in the long span and 6.3 in the short span and the hogging minus 35 at B.

examples.question: A continuous beam has two spans, AB = 6 m and BC = 4 m, with simple supports at A and C and a continuous support at B. A uniformly distributed load w = 10 kN/m acts on both spans. Find the bending moment at B.
steps: L₁ = 6 m, L₂ = 4 m, w = 10 kN/m. Simple ends give M<sub>A</sub> = 0 and M<sub>C</sub> = 0.
For a simple span under UDL, A = wL³/12 and 6Ax̄/L = wL³/4. For AB: 10 × 6³ / 4 = 540 kN·m². For BC: 10 × 4³ / 4 = 160 kN·m².
examples.answer: M<sub>B</sub> = −35 kN·m, a hogging moment at support B.

examples.question: The same two-span beam (AB = 6 m, BC = 4 m, simple ends A and C) now carries a 40 kN point load at the middle of AB and a 30 kN point load at the middle of BC. Find M<sub>B</sub>, the reactions and the largest sagging moments.
steps: Right side for central point loads: −(3P₁L₁² + 3P₂L₂²)/8 = −(3 × 40 × 36 + 3 × 30 × 16)/8 = −(4320 + 1440)/8 = −720.
Left side with M<sub>A</sub> = M<sub>C</sub> = 0: 2M<sub>B</sub>(6 + 4) = 20M<sub>B</sub>. So M<sub>B</sub> = −720/20 = −36 kN·m (hogging).
Span AB as a free body: R<sub>A</sub> = 40/2 + M<sub>B</sub>/6 = 20 − 6 = 14 kN; the B end takes 20 + 6 = 26 kN.
Span BC: R<sub>C</sub> = 30/2 + M<sub>B</sub>/4 = 15 − 9 = 6 kN; the B end takes 15 + 9 = 24 kN. R<sub>B</sub> = 26 + 24 = 50 kN. Check: 14 + 50 + 6 = 70 kN.
Sagging under the loads: AB at 3 m, M = 14 × 3 = 42 kN·m; BC at 2 m from C, M = 6 × 2 = 12 kN·m. The free moments PL/4 were 60 and 30 kN·m; half of M<sub>B</sub> (18) comes off each.
examples.answer: M<sub>B</sub> = −36 kN·m; reactions 14, 50 and 6 kN; largest sagging moment 42 kN·m under the 40 kN load.

traps: Losing the sign: a hogging moment at an intermediate support is negative when sagging is positive.
Measuring x̄ from B instead of the outer support A or C.
Forgetting that a simple end has M = 0 but a fixed end has an unknown M.
Using the total beam length instead of each span length separately.

quiz.q: State Clapeyron's three-moment equation for spans L₁ and L₂.
quiz.a: M<sub>A</sub> L₁ + 2M<sub>B</sub>(L₁ + L₂) + M<sub>C</sub> L₂ = −6(A₁x̄₁/L₁ + A₂x̄₂/L₂).

quiz.q: Why does a simply supported end simplify the equation?
quiz.a: Its support moment is zero, so one unknown and its term disappear.

quiz.q: Two simple-ended spans, 5 m and 3 m, carry UDL 8 kN/m on both. Find M<sub>B</sub>.
A fixed end at A changes what in the equation?
quiz.a: M<sub>A</sub> is no longer zero. Add an imaginary span of zero length and no load beyond A and write the three-moment equation across it: 2M<sub>A</sub> L₁ + M<sub>B</sub> L₁ = −6A₁x̄₁/L₁, measured from B. That is the extra equation.

quiz.q: For a central point load P on one simple span L, what is the right-side term?
Why is the centroid measured from the outer support?
quiz.a: The derivation takes moments of the free bending moment diagram about the outer supports A and C, so x̄₁ is from A and x̄₂ is from C.

beyond: Not for the exam. Commercial frame analysis software builds the same equations in matrix form for hundreds of supports. Settlement, temperature and varying EI add terms that this unit leaves out. Searching 'three-moment equation settlement' or 'Clapeyron theorem continuous beam' leads to those extensions.
